templates.logline: A boy of twelve keeps a private account of everything his father sells.
templates.source_doc: The Second Ledger - Series Bible

character.name: Abel van Haren
character.default_clothing: plain dark 17th-century Dutch merchant's-son wool coat, linen collar, buckled shoes
character.default_expression: watchful, unbearably polite
character.one_line: Twelve, small for it, Dutch-pale and sunburnt. His mother's piety and his father's arithmetic, at war in one boy. His one power is that nobody counts him.

engine.premise: Abel van Haren, 12, sails with his charming slave-factor father Cornelis down the African coast, across the Atlantic and home. His father gives him a blank ledger to learn double-entry bookkeeping; Abel instead keeps a SECOND ledger — left column what the world says a person is worth (a man, prime, f140), right column the person's NAME and what they told him. He cannot free anyone or stop a single sale. He can only see, count, and refuse to let the arithmetic be the only record. The horror is that his father's books BALANCE perfectly; the evil is not in the arithmetic, so where is it? He audits, line by line, looking for the entry where the world went wrong.
engine.episode_format: ~12-18 min. Six beats: (1) The Question Abel writes at the top of the page at dawn [title card]; (2) The Ordinary ~20% ship/shore business, the father being lovable — never skip it, the ordinariness delivers the horror; (3) The Evidence ~30% the day gives him something he did not want; (4) The Pressure ~20% he must participate, stay silent, or choose; (5) The Entry ~15% night, the ledger, his answer + three self-objections; (6) The Undefeated Objection ~10% the third objection stands — that is tomorrow's hook (rotate intellectual / emotional / physical).
engine.generative_machinery: Draw one from each: (A) a QUESTION SEED from the bank of 30 (e.g. 'Is a promise to a man you own still a promise?', 'Can a thing be lawful and also a crime?', 'If everyone does it, is any of it mine?', 'Is mercy that changes nothing still mercy?'); (B) an EPISODE TYPE from the wheel of 12 (The Name, The Argument, The Good Day, The Small Mercy, The Backfire, The Near-Discovery, The Silence, The Machine, The Mirror, The Text, The Body, The Letter); (C) a RELATIONSHIP PRESSURE; (D) a COMPLICATION; (E) a HOOK TYPE. Never the same episode type twice in three days. Five fuel engines run in parallel: Question, Name, Father, Complicity, Small Mercy.
rules: Abel NEVER frees anyone — he is a powerless child; the premise dies if he becomes a rescuer.
The enslaved characters are people, never instruments: names always, interiority independent of Abel, no gratitude, agency including refusal.
Consequence, not spectacle — violence conveyed through aftermath, sound, silence, paperwork.
The father is charming in every episode he appears in, including the worst ones.
Abel loses every argument he has out loud; he wins only on the page, alone, at night, too late.
No borrowed morality — his objections built only from tools available in 1672 (Scripture, Roman law, Grotius, Descartes, Montaigne, Spinoza, his own eyes).
History is fixed; the trade continues. Never imply 'different times'. The ledger is never presented as sufficient.

question_seeds: Is a promise made to a man you own still a promise?
Can a thing be lawful and also a crime?
If everyone does it, is any of it mine?
Does the last pair of hands carry all the guilt, or none?
What is a name for, if no one will use it?
Is it worse to do harm, or to profit from harm you did not do?
Can you be kind inside a cruelty without excusing it?
Why is a bad man's argument sometimes better than a good man's?
If I record it and change nothing, what have I done?
Is my father one man or two?
What does a good man look like from below?
Does the sea care? Should that comfort me or not?
Who invented the price? Who agreed to it?
Can a book be wrong if it is Scripture?
Is obedience a virtue if the order is monstrous?
Am I a witness or a spectator? What is the difference?
Is silence a lie?
If I would not do it to one man, why can I watch it done to four hundred?
Does counting people help them, or only me?
What do I owe someone I cannot help?
Is guilt useful, or only comfortable?
Would I refuse if refusing cost me nothing?
Can a machine be evil if every part of it is innocent?
Is mercy that changes nothing still mercy?
Who is my neighbour, if not the man beneath the deck I sleep on?
Why do I find the honest brute easier to bear than the gentle scholar?
If I inherit this, when exactly did it become mine?
Does a man consent when his king sells him?
Is a question a form of cowardice?
What is the smallest thing that is still something?

arcs.name: The Outbound
arcs.where: Amsterdam, Texel, the Atlantic, Cape Verde
arcs.spine: Road story. A boy learns a machine. The Hague lynching; departure; the ship is beautiful and the men are good company. No enslaved person seen until ep 71 — before that it is paperwork, and worse.

arcs.name: The Coast
arcs.where: Elmina, Axim, Shama, the Slave Coast
arcs.spine: Castle intrigue, dense character work. Waiting, bargaining, credit, disease, the chapel above the cells. Kofi and Ma Efua enter; Coppens disappears.

arcs.name: The Crossing
arcs.spine: Confinement thriller. 60-odd days, nowhere to go. Restraint, sound, indirection, consequence over spectacle. Abel's ledger nearly kills him twice.

arcs.name: The Islands
arcs.spine: Colonial gothic. Numbers become fields. Auctions, plantations, maroons. Abel discovers he is now, legally, of an age to own.

arcs.name: The Reckoning
arcs.spine: Family drama & trial. Home unbearable because unchanged. His mother's orphanage; the firm's books; Spinoza who will not give an answer. The countdown runs out.

serialization.countdown: On his 16th birthday (ep 500) Abel must sign the company register in his own hand — becoming a man in law and a partner, at which point his secret ledger becomes evidence against himself. He signs. Announce in ep 3, mention rarely.
recurring_cast: Cornelis van Haren (father, slave factor — must be loved)
Kofi (12, taken, sharper than Abel, survives, has a plan)
Dr. Reinier Sloot (ship's surgeon, Abel's dark mirror)
Bastiaan Voogt (the father's brutal, honest factor)
Meester Barend Coppens (tutor — vanishes at Elmina)
long_mysteries: The marginalia — another hand writes single-line questions in Abel's ledger at night.
What happened to Coppens (fled, killed, or defected).
The first voyage — Cornelis on a ship in 1658 nobody will discuss.
Kofi's plan (set up Arc II, pays off Arc IV).
The dowry — Abel's mother's money financed the ship.

engine.premise: Kareem works a volunteer rubble-recovery crew — six men, a boy, hand tools, a generator and a rope — that families hire to open a collapsed building. One building per episode; one family; one thing found or not found. He goes into the voids the adults can't fit through.

Personal — Kareem's own building reaches the top of the list.

character.one_line: Zin Ko Latt, 20. Knows nine ways across the river and which two are currently survivable.

engine.premise: Zin Ko runs a route: medicine, insulin and cash one way; people escaping conscription the other. Not a soldier, not exactly a smuggler — logistics, which in this war is a lifeline. One crossing per episode: one cargo, one passenger, one set of checkpoints, one thing that goes wrong.

Medicine — a cargo of insulin overheats; someone downstream dies for it.
Scam compounds — a mother pays everything to get her son out of a compound she can see across the river.
Air war — the ford is struck the night before a crossing, with 40 already waiting.
Personal — the route is compromised; working out by whom takes a season.
engine.why_it_hooks: A road movie that renews itself every night, in a country where each checkpoint is a different regime.

character.default_expression: watchful, competent, carrying more than a person that age should

engine.premise: Chance is a chargeur: he carries other people's goods across the Goma-Gisenyi border for a few hundred francs a trip. Because he is nine, small, cheerful and known, he moves through checkpoints that stop everyone else — so people start giving him other things to carry: messages, money, medicine, news. One crossing, one cargo, one client per episode.

Education — a displaced teacher starts running lessons for the children in the line.

character.one_line: Saleh Qaid, 14. Works for a money changer and can do the day's cross-rate in his head faster than the machine.

engine.premise: Saleh works the counter and runs the notes, back and forth across a de facto frontier between two central banks and two versions of the same currency. One transaction per episode. The counter is a confessional — people have to say exactly what the money is for — and the exchange rate itself is the war.

Detention — Saleh's employer is arrested, and Saleh knows where everything is.
Recruitment — a recruiter offers Saleh a salary in the stronger currency.

character.one_line: Halima Bukar, 22. Taken at seventeen, released at nineteen, and now the only person both sides will speak to.

engine.premise: Halima negotiates. Abducted at 17, held two years, she came back with fluency in how the other side thinks and a phone number. Families come to her when someone is taken, and she brokers the price. One abduction, one negotiation, one family per episode, with a clock and a number that moves. She is never in the room where the violence happens — only on the phone, doing arithmetic with a life.

Japa — the money is coming from a nurse in Manchester who cannot get leave to come home.

character.one_line: Emilia Zambrano, 15. Takes the register in 4B, and has started keeping a second one.

engine.premise: Emilia takes the attendance register for her class, then starts a second, private one: WHY. Moved to Spain. Working. Pregnant. Scared. Recruited. Dead. One empty chair per episode — a complete story about one family, told by a 15-year-old trying to understand what is happening to everyone she grew up with.

Energy — a 14-hour blackout the night before exams; half the class hasn't revised.

templates.series_title: Farnah, or The Boy Who Remembers Forward
templates.logline: A boy at a waystation answers any question about the future in stories — and every story costs him one memory of his own.
templates.setting: A caravan waystation below Ecbatana, Media, 550-546 BC (tales span c.650 BC-2030 AD)
templates.source_doc: FARNAH - series premise

character.name: Farnah, son of Vahyazdata
character.default_clothing: plain 6th-c. BC Median waystation boy's tunic, wool wrap, sandals
character.default_expression: watchful, unbearably polite; frightened and covering it by explaining things
character.one_line: Twelve, small, watchful. Remembers backwards a century of Median history he never lived — and remembers FORWARD 2,600 years the same way, as things already over.

engine.premise: In the year Cyrus takes Ecbatana, Farnah, 12, at his grandmother's caravan waystation on what will become the Royal Road, discovers he can answer any question about the future — in STORIES. A traveller arrives daily with a problem and asks. Farnah answers with a nested tale drawn from any point between c.650 BC and 2030 AD; the tale IS the episode and resolves completely. Each telling costs him one memory of his own — the further forward, the more expensive. He is filling up with everyone else's past and running out of room for his own.
engine.episode_format: Standard daily A/B/C ~60/30/10. A = the self-contained nested tale (any century; a new viewer can arrive on any Tuesday). B = the frame arc (the King's Eye, the wax tablet, the magus, the queue in the yard) advanced 5-10%. C = a slow burn (Roshanak, the Bactrian, Kleon's manuscript) one scene a fortnight, paying off ~18 months later. Variable cost dial: bottle weeks in the waystation, event weeks a thousand on a hillside.
engine.generative_machinery: A traveller a day, a question a day, a century a day. THE QUESTION CHOOSES THE CENTURY, and the century must JUMP — no two consecutive episodes in the same era, no era more than four times in any twenty. Tonal week: Monday warm, Tuesday funny, Wednesday heavy, Thursday frame-and-arc, Friday cliffhanger. Material bank = 2,680 years, 11 state formations, 5 religions, every invasion route.
rules: He must be asked — no question, no vision (the road is the engine, not the boy).
He answers with a story, not a prediction — he can say what happened, not what to do; the listener must decide.
He cannot see his own life or the life of anyone he loves.
Every telling costs him a memory of his own (this is the clock and the tragedy).
He cannot see what he changes — the future he remembers does not update; he never knows if he is remembering history or writing it.
He is never wrong, and frequently disbelieved — information 200 years early is not power, it is noise.
TWO DATABASES: a story-ledger (every tale used, tagged by era/region/beat, so it never repeats) and a chronicle (contradiction-checked spine, because he is never wrong).

arcs.name: Year 1 - The Discovery
arcs.spine: Cyrus takes Ecbatana. A Median officer asks whether he should die fighting; word travels; by mid-year there is a queue in the yard — and a queue is a business.

arcs.name: Year 2 - The State Arrives
arcs.spine: The King's Eye takes a room and never leaves. Farnah becomes an instrument of administration; he cannot remember his father's face; the grandmother begins the wax tablet.

arcs.name: Year 3 - The Trial of the Fire
arcs.spine: The magus's question: servant of Truth or of the Lie? A theological hearing with an open verdict. A Greek scribe starts writing Farnah down — and getting him wrong.

arcs.name: Year 4 - The King's Three Questions
arcs.spine: Farnah is taken to Cyrus, who asks how long it lasts, how it ends, how he dies. Farnah answers two honestly and lies about the third (told ~ep 740-equivalent; audience knows it's a lie).

arcs.name: Year 5 - Sardis, and the Crack
arcs.spine: Lydia falls; it becomes an empire. Farnah notices a discrepancy in the taking of Sardis that does not match his memory: is he remembering the future, or building it?

banked_years: 539 BC Babylon - the Cyrus Cylinder written in a room he stands in.
530 BC Cyrus dies on campaign; Farnah, 23, learns whether his lie held.
525-522 BC Egypt, Cambyses, a succession crisis - a boy who knows the future becomes a weapon.
520 BC Behistun - Darius carves his lie into a cliff; the natural end of the series.
recurring_cast: Amytis, 63 (grandmother, runs the waystation, keeps the wax tablet)
Datis, 17 (brother, soldier of the new king, correct about money)
Vahuka, 48 (the magus who keeps the fire - the show's conscience)
Bagabigna, 44 (the King's Eye - imperial intelligence, genuinely fond of Farnah)
Kleon of Miletos, 34 (Greek scribe - writes it down and gets it wrong)
The Bactrian (caravan master, every ~40 days, asks his questions in an order)
Roshanak, 11 (Babylonian girl - the one relationship that is not transactional)
